newsitem.title: USA: Leading Georgia Republican admits to adultery.
newsitem.headline: Leading Georgia Republican admits to adultery.

text.p: The leading Republican candidate for governor of Georgia admitted on Thursday to having a decade-long adulterous affair while enforcing state laws against adultery and sodomy when he was attorney general.

Mike Bowers, who resigned as the state's top legal official to run for governor this year, said he would remain in the race despite an affair that led him and his wife to separate temporarily. But he resigned his major general's commission in the state Air National Guard to protect the service from potential repercussions.

"I'm very ashamed and I regret (this) very much, most especially in terms of the hurt I've caused. I can't envision that hurt getting healed by my going ahead and doing this. And I know I can't get out from under the guilt," the 55-year-old Bowers said in disclosing the affair with a woman who worked in his office in the early 1980s.

He said it continued for 10 years, even after she left to take another job. He refused to identify the woman but said the affair caused him to separate from his wife of 33 years, Bette Rose. The two have since reconciled.

Bowers, a West Point graduate, has broad popularity among Georgia's conservative voters largely because of his reputation for moral integrity and ethical conduct. As attorney general, he waged a vigorous campaign to uphold traditional sexual mores, an effort that won him praise from Republican constituents but also earned him the ire of the state's gay and lesbian community.

The most famous case involved a lesbian from whom he withdrew a job offer in 1991 after learning that she planned to marry her partner. His decision was upheld last week in a federal appellate court in Atlanta.

As the only formal Republican gubernatorial candidate for next year's election, Bowers has pledged to run for office on a strong family-values platform. Republican officials in Georgia said they did not expect the revelation of his adultery to dampen party enthusiasm for Bowers in the primary.
Asked how he believed voters would respond, Bowers said: "I don't know. I do not know the answer to that. That's in the hands of the people, and I will accept their judgment."
